title: private-net-egress-heuristics-scratch
body:
Purpose: quick scratchpad while iterating on a recurring private-deploy customer incident. Focus: intermittent outgoing TLS failures from nodes in peered VPCs when hitting external vendor endpoints. This is a personal running log (commands I ran, snippets, hypotheses, and next steps).

Summary of symptom:
- Customer reports 5-10% of outbound requests from model servers to external logging/metrics vendors fail with TLS handshake errors. Fails are bursty but correlate with scale-up events and NAT churn.
- Failure modes observed: TLS handshake timeout, certificate name mismatch (client saw IP in SNI mismatch), and sporadic TCP RST immediately after SYN-ACK.

Environments checked:
- Private deployment in us-west-2, VPC peered to management VPC (transit-like).
- Nodes run on k8s with egress via NAT instances for some subnets and via shared NAT gateways for others.

Commands and raw outputs (redacted IPs and hostnames):
1) DNS check from a failing pod (kubectl exec -> busybox):
$ nslookup metrics.vendor.example.com
Server: 10.0.0.2
Address: 10.0.0.2#53
Name: metrics.vendor.example.com
Address: 34.200.122.51
Name: metrics.vendor.example.com
Address: 52.34.11.9

Observation: split-horizon DNS; internal resolver returns public IPs (expected). No TTL issues.

2) curl verbose to observe TLS:
$ curl -v --resolve metrics.vendor.example.com:443:34.200.122.51 https://metrics.vendor.example.com/api/ingest -o /dev/null
* Rebuilt URL to: https://metrics.vendor.example.com/api/ingest
*   Trying 34.200.122.51...
* TCP_NODELAY set
* Connected to metrics.vendor.example.com (34.200.122.51) port 443 (#0)
* TLS 1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):
* TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Server hello (2):
* TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Encrypted Extensions (8):
* TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Certificate (11):
* TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, CERT verify (15):
* TLS 1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Finished (20):
* TLS 1.3 (OUT), TLS change cipher, Change cipher spec (1):
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
* Server certificate: subject: CN=*.vendor.example.com
* subjectAltName: host "metrics.vendor.example.com" matched cert's "*.vendor.example.com"
> POST /api/ingest HTTP/2
> Host: metrics.vendor.example.com
...
* Connection #0 to host metrics.vendor.example.com left intact

Works for this instance.

3) Replicate failure (observed on node where requests timeout):
$ openssl s_client -connect 34.200.122.51:443 -servername metrics.vendor.example.com -brief
CONNECTED(00000003)
140736...:error:1425F102:SSL routines:ssl_choose_client_version:unsupported protocol
---
no peer certificate available
---

Interpretation: a TLS negotiation aborted early. sometimes openssl reports unsupported protocol which is suspicious given server supports TLS1.3. Could be middlebox interfering or SYN reaching different backend (port-proxy returning reset).

4) TCP-level traces on host (tshark/tcpdump) during reproduction window:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 34.200.122.51 and port 443 -w /tmp/trace.pcap

Snippet (interpreted):
- 3 out of 10 TCP sessions complete handshake and proceed. 7 show SYN -> SYN-ACK -> immediate RST from source (client) or sometimes RST from an intermediate NAT.
- When RST originates from client, kernel conntrack sometimes had entries in TIME_WAIT or existing flows to other IPs which looked like ephemeral port reuse clash.

5) Conntrack inspect:
$ sudo conntrack -L | egrep "dst=34.200.122.51|dst=52.34.11.9" | tail -n 20
tcp      6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.0.5.23 dst=34.200.122.51 sport=51118 dport=443 ...
(large list, many CLOSE_WAIT / TIME_WAIT entries)

Hypothesis 1: NAT port exhaustion / ephemeral port reuse causing packets to be misclassified (late packets mapped to new flows) leading to RSTs and aborted TLS. When autoscaling triggers, many short-lived connections spawn and some ports get recycled while packets still in flight.

Hypothesis 2: Asymmetric routing through peered VPC plus TTL/DF anomalies. Some replies return via a different NAT or transit instance that does not have conntrack state leading to RST or ICMP unreachable, collapsing TLS handshake.

Hypothesis 3: Split-horizon or proxy rewriting SNI/header; unusual case where internal egress proxy sends 503 or TCP-level reset for blacklisted IP ranges. But vendor confirmed no filtering on their side.

Quick experiments tried and outcomes:
- Increase ephemeral port range on NAT instance (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range) to a larger window -> reduced frequency but did not eliminate.
- Forced source route using iptables SNAT to ensure single NAT IP per subnet -> seemed to reduce asymmetric returns but still sporadic failures.
- Disabled TCP timestamps on host (net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps=0) to see if timestamp mismatch impacted NAT timeouts -> inconclusive.
- Added iptables rule to log and DROP RSTs generated by local stack for a short window to see if helpful -> saw fewer handshake aborts but this is a bandaid.

Vendor-side checks:
- Vendor confirmed their backends are behind a load-balancer that terminates TLS and frontends are in multiple AZs. No known rate-limiting observed for this customer.
- Vendor saw retries from different source IPs which matched hypothesis of ephemeral SNAT changing.

Relevant config snippets on NAT hosts: (redacted)
- iptables MASQUERADE on eth0 with conntrack helpers enabled.
- keepalive timeouts: conntrack_tcp_timeout_established 432000.

Observations that feel important:
- Failures spike during k8s scale-up when pods are created across multiple subnets, causing uneven NAT mapping.
- Nodes that consistently work are pinned to a single NAT gateway (less churn).
- Failed TLS sessions often have a tiny gap (50-200ms) between SYN-ACK and subsequent client behavior; suggests packet reorder or late retransmit handling.

Next investigative steps (todo):
- Produce synchronized packet captures from client node, NAT host, and vendor-facing interface for same connection id. Use tcpreplay-style correlation via TCP timestamps and sequence numbers.
- Temporarily route all egress for one failing k8s node through a dedicated NAT instance with increased ephemeral range to see if failures go away fully.
- Add kernel option to log conntrack (+nf_conntrack events) to see when flows get garbage-collected relative to new SYNs.
- Ask vendor to provide timestamps for observed failing TLS sessions (if they keep logs keyed by client IP and request id). Match with our captured SYNs.
- Check for any inline MTU clamping on peering devices that may cause fragmentation and retransmit behaviour. Run mtr with packet-size tuning.

Known mitigations to propose to customer (short-term):
- Pin critical egress traffic to stable NAT gateway (route via dedicated egress subnet) until root cause is determined.
- Configure client-side exponential backoff and retry with idempotency for non-critical telemetry to mitigate transient handshake failures.

Notes and loose ideas:
- Could be interaction between AWS internal ELB health checks and stateful AWS NAT behaviors (some historical posts about NAT gateway dropping flows if ephemeral port reused while connection still half-closed).
- Consider swapping NAT gateway to managed AWS NAT Gateway if currently using custom NAT instances; managed service might handle bursts differently. But managed gateway has different cost profile and sometimes different behaviour for high ephemeral reuse.
